candidates.title: Controlled isolation with a rehearsed recovery routine
candidates.proposal:
Use one-change-at-a-time trials to identify which recoverable state accompanies the disconnection, then retain only an intervention that shows repeatable benefit. This needs the existing cable, outlet, queue view, printing application and blank or synthetic document; no installation or privileged settings.

Reserve about 40 minutes after hours. Begin only when authorized staff confirm that both the queue and printer have no outstanding client jobs. Observe counts and status without opening documents, previews or job details. Use an explicitly synthetic page if the application suppresses empty pages.

Run this sequence, recording connection status, queue progress and whether each test page emerges:

1. Baseline: send two identical test jobs separately, with a short idle interval.
2. Queue: if a test stalls, cancel only that synthetic job using ordinary user controls, wait for removal, then repeat. If cancellation is unavailable, stop that branch.
3. Application: close and reopen the same application with only the test document, then repeat. Improvement supports an application-state explanation; shared driver faults remain unresolved.
4. Cable: with no jobs pending, disconnect and firmly reconnect the existing USB cable, remove obvious tension, and repeat. Improvement supports the USB connection path, but cannot distinguish contact trouble from USB re-enumeration.
5. Power/device: with no pending jobs, perform a normal printer power-off/on at the existing outlet and repeat. Improvement supports a device/reset-sensitive explanation; it does not establish an outlet fault because restarting also resets software.

Keep the original port, outlet and settings. Restore cable routing after the comparison if safe. Recreate canceled synthetic jobs when needed; never clear the whole queue.

For opening day, rehearse the shortest successful recovery while the system is empty, then verify readiness with one synthetic page. Submit client jobs individually. If disconnection recurs, pause submissions and have authorized staff reconcile job status before resending, avoiding duplicate confidential output.
candidates.experiment: Compare each intervention with the immediately preceding identical test. Rechallenge any apparent improvement with the same job and idle interval. A recurrence falsifies the claim that the intervention reliably fixes it. If baseline never fails, report ��not reproduced�� and retain only the readiness check and pause/reconcile fallback. No cable substitution, electrical measurement or driver-level diagnosis is available; intermittent faults may remain unresolved.

candidates.title: Prevent an idle-triggered disconnect through attended printing windows
candidates.proposal:
Test whether inactivity triggers the failure, then organize printing around the successful awake state. This changes when the connection is used; the prior route primarily restores it after failure. It requires only the existing computer, printer, queue view and synthetic document, with an office staff member owning a 40-minute after-hours session.

Start when authorized staff confirm there are no outstanding client jobs or uncollected pages. Observe only queue counts/status and printer indicators. Use a synthetic page if blank pages are suppressed. Keep the cable, outlet and application unchanged.

Compare three conditions: send a synthetic page after five minutes with the computer untouched; repeat after five minutes while keeping the computer awake through harmless queue interaction; then send two synthetic pages close together while the computer remains awake. Repeat the most informative comparison if time permits. The first comparison tests computer inactivity; the second explores printer inactivity, although elapsed time remains a competing explanation.

At a failure, record whether the printer remains powered, whether the queue receives the job, and whether it subsequently advances. Reconcile and cancel only synthetic jobs before proceeding. Reopen the application and retry; if still unsuccessful, reseat the existing USB cable and retry; finally, perform a normal printer power cycle and retry. Stop a branch if ordinary controls cannot clear its synthetic job. These probes distinguish observable queue, application, connection and device states; cable and power-sensitive electronics may remain unresolved.

If keeping the computer awake repeatedly helps, use brief, attended printing windows next day. If only closely spaced printing succeeds, begin each window with a synthetic readiness page and release waiting work promptly. Staff retain control of client submissions and reconcile failures before any resend. Restore the original idle behavior after testing.
candidates.experiment: Compare two matched idle intervals, then repeat the apparent successful condition against ordinary operation using the prior route��s shortest recovery if needed. Record completed synthetic jobs, interruptions, staff attention and wasted pages. Reject the prevention routine if it offers no repeatable improvement or requires impractical attention. Stop at 40 minutes, an unexpected client job, or uncertain job cancellation. If no failure occurs, report ��not reproduced��; use a readiness check and pause/reconcile fallback without claiming an idle diagnosis.

candidates.title: Reduce failures by changing job packaging
candidates.proposal:
Test whether job size or job boundaries trigger the interruption, then use the more reliable submission pattern. A rendering or spooling fault could depend on packaging even when cable reseating or power cycling temporarily restores service. Unlike the prior route��s recovery sequence, this route changes the workload entering the queue.

An office staff member owns a 35-minute after-hours trial. Prerequisites are an empty queue confirmed by authorized staff, no uncollected client output, and an existing application whose print dialog supports copies or page ranges. Create three identical synthetic pages; inspect no client documents. Keep the outlet, cable, application, content and print settings fixed.

Compare one three-page job with three one-page jobs, submitting each separate job only after the preceding one completes. Repeat in reverse order, allowing at most twelve comparison pages. This tests a practical submission policy; it cannot distinguish packaging from the pacing introduced by waiting.

For each block, observe whether jobs enter the queue, leave it and produce the expected synthetic page count, alongside the printer��s power indicator. If a failure occurs, stop submissions and reconcile synthetic output. Cancel only the synthetic job if permitted, then retry one page. Next reopen the application and retry; then reseat the existing USB cable with the queue empty; finally perform a normal printer power cycle and retry. Queue-only recovery, application-only recovery, connection-sensitive recovery and device-reset recovery support different explanations, with shared driver and cable/power ambiguities recorded explicitly. Stop if a job cannot be safely reconciled.

Next day, use the winning packaging only where staff can apply it through ordinary print controls. Document owners select their own page ranges if needed. Track completed ranges without recording contents, and reconcile uncertain output before resending. If smaller jobs provide no benefit, retain ordinary submissions and the shortest successful recovery.
candidates.experiment: Compare successful pages and interruptions across both packaging policies, plus submission time, counting effort and duplicate or missing synthetic pages. Inspect every synthetic block for correct completion. Prefer smaller jobs only if their repeatable reliability benefit justifies the extra handling; one successful block is insufficient. Stop at 35 minutes, unexpected client work or uncertain output status. If failures never reproduce, report packaging sensitivity as unproven. The principal shifted risk is page-range error, so abandon splitting if staff cannot track ranges reliably.

candidates.title: Choose a recovery only after checking for spontaneous recovery
candidates.proposal:
Upgrade of ��Controlled isolation with a rehearsed recovery routine.�� Preserve its queue, application, cable and printer-power sequence, but add a bounded observation period before each intervention. The consequential change is that recovery during this period does not justify adding a reset to the next-day procedure. An intermittent fault might otherwise disappear just as someone reseats the cable.

One authorized staff member owns a maximum 40-minute after-hours session. Use the existing cable, outlet, queue view and blank document; add a simple synthetic mark only if blank pages are suppressed. Begin after staff confirm no outstanding client jobs or uncollected client output. Observe queue counts/status without opening job details or previews.

Send two separate synthetic jobs with a short idle interval. At a stall, stop submissions and observe for 60 seconds without changing anything. If the pending job completes, record spontaneous recovery and repeat the baseline once. Do not send another copy while completion remains uncertain.

If the fault persists, proceed through the original sequence: cancel only the synthetic job using ordinary controls and retry; close and reopen the test application and retry; with the queue empty and synthetic output accounted for, reseat the existing USB cable and remove tension; finally perform a normal printer power cycle at the same outlet. Before each intervention, apply the same observation period. Stop if a pending job cannot be reconciled or ordinary controls are insufficient. Retain the original port, outlet and settings, and restore safe cable routing after the comparison.

Queue-only recovery supports a queue-state explanation; application-only recovery supports application state; USB reseating supports a connection/reset-sensitive explanation; printer restarting supports a device/reset-sensitive explanation. These observations cannot independently establish a defective cable, outlet or driver.

For opening day, the same staff member retains only the least disruptive recovery with repeated supporting observations. Start with one synthetic readiness page. During client printing, pause at a recurrence and reconcile accepted jobs and output counts before recovery or resubmission. If job state remains uncertain, defer printing. Compared with immediately trying every reset, this adds waiting but may avoid unnecessary interventions and duplicate output.
candidates.experiment: Record synthetic jobs accepted, pages produced, queue progression, printer power indicators and recovery before versus after intervention. Within 40 minutes, repeat the strongest apparent recovery once if another persistent failure occurs; do not manufacture a failure. Adopt it provisionally only if persistent failures recover after that action on two occasions and the observation periods do not explain the apparent benefit. Otherwise label the intervention unconfirmed. Stop on unexpected client work, uncertain output or the time limit. If no failure occurs, report ��not reproduced�� and use the readiness check plus pause/reconcile fallback. No cable substitution, electrical measurement or privileged software diagnosis is available.

candidates.title: Make attended printing depend on a matched idle comparison
candidates.proposal:
Upgrade of ��Prevent an idle-triggered disconnect through attended printing windows.�� Preserve its prevention mechanism and recovery probes, but measure both comparison intervals from the last completed page. Its original comparison can otherwise confuse computer activity with different printer idle durations. The changed operating decision is to require a successful readiness page after another substantial idle period, rather than assuming that keeping the computer awake guarantees printer readiness.

An authorized staff member owns one 40-minute after-hours session, using the existing computer, printer, cable, outlet, queue view and synthetic document. Begin with no outstanding client jobs or uncollected client output. Keep all settings unchanged and remain present during the active condition.

After a successful synthetic page, leave the computer untouched for five minutes, then submit one synthetic page. After recovery and another successful page, wait the same five minutes while using harmless queue interactions to keep the computer active, then submit the identical page. Count each interval from page completion, not submission. Reverse the order once if time permits. If the untouched condition never actually reaches the suspected inactivity state, record that limitation; do not change sleep or security settings to force it.

At a persistent failure, stop submissions and reconcile synthetic output. Try canceling only the synthetic job, then reopening the test application, then reseating the USB cable with the queue empty, and finally normal printer power-off/on. Observe queue progress and power indicators after each step. Stop if cancellation or output accounting is uncertain. These probes retain separate queue, application, connection and device-reset observations, while leaving driver, cable and outlet causes unresolved.

Use attended printing windows next day only if the active condition repeatedly succeeds where the matched untouched condition fails. Start each window with a successful synthetic page; after five minutes without printing, repeat that check before accepting more work. This is a conservative operating rule for the tested interval, not a discovered timeout threshold. If readiness fails, use the shortest supported recovery only after pending work is reconciled; otherwise defer printing. Compared with ordinary submissions, this may reduce idle-associated interruptions but consumes staff attention and extra pages.
candidates.experiment: Compare completed synthetic jobs, interruptions, page counts and staff effort across matched five-minute intervals. Prefer the attended routine only if the difference repeats in both trial orders and the daily attention cost is acceptable. If both conditions fail, keeping the computer active is insufficient; if both succeed, the prevention benefit is unproven. Stop at 40 minutes, unexpected client work or unresolved output. If recovery consumes the remaining time, report an incomplete comparison and use only the readiness and pause/reconcile fallback. Longer idle periods and infrequent failures remain untested.

candidates.title: Use an operating-system test page to bypass the document application
candidates.proposal:
New mechanism: compare two existing ways of generating a print job. An operating-system printer test page bypasses the document application's rendering path while retaining much of the queue, driver, USB and printer path. This can support a narrower software diagnosis without first resetting the shared connection.

One authorized staff member owns a maximum 35-minute after-hours session. This route requires the existing queue interface to expose an ordinary-user test-page command. Check availability first; do not install anything, change configuration or seek elevated access. If unavailable, this route cannot make its distinguishing comparison: use a synthetic readiness page and the bounded queue/application/cable/power recovery sequence below, reporting application bypass as untested.

Start with no outstanding client jobs or uncollected client output. Use only the empty document, or a simple synthetic mark if necessary, and the operating system's generated test page. Do not open client jobs, previews or document details. Keep the cable, outlet and print settings fixed.

Print one application-generated synthetic page and one operating-system test page separately, accounting for each before proceeding. Repeat in reverse order. At an application-job failure, reconcile and cancel only that synthetic job if permitted, then try the operating-system page before reopening the application. If the operating-system page succeeds, reopen the original application and retry its synthetic document. Repeated operating-system success alongside application failure supports an application or application-specific rendering explanation; the pages differ, so it does not prove the application alone is defective.

If both paths fail, examine queue state and try ordinary cancellation of only the synthetic job. With the queue empty and output accounted for, test USB reseating, then a normal printer power cycle at the existing outlet. Record each recovery separately. Stop if job state cannot be reconciled. These observations distinguish application-associated failure from shared-path failure, with cable, driver and power ambiguities stated explicitly.

For opening day, if reopening the application repeatedly restores its synthetic printing while the operating-system path remains functional, staff use that application restart before accepting client work after a recurrence. If its synthetic check still fails, defer client printing rather than treating a successful operating-system page as sufficient readiness. For shared-path failures, retain only a supported recovery. Compared with repeated cable or power resets, this route may avoid unnecessary connection interruptions, at the cost of extra test pages and a test-page command that may be unavailable.
candidates.experiment: Run at most two application/operating-system pairs, plus one pair after an apparent application recovery, within 35 minutes. Record job acceptance, queue progress, completed synthetic pages and power indicators. Application-only failure in both orders supports the narrower software explanation; failure on both paths directs attention to their shared components. A successful operating-system page followed by another failed application page rejects readiness for normal document printing. Stop on unexpected client work, unavailable ordinary controls, uncertain output or the time limit. No tests have been run; successful comparisons cannot exclude rare faults, and driver internals, electrical quality and replacement-cable performance remain unchecked.

candidates.title: Bypass a suspect computer USB port with a reversible crossover
candidates.proposal:
Change the physical USB endpoint on the existing computer. If another compatible built-in port is available, moving the same cable can bypass a faulty socket or a port-specific connection problem. Previous trials kept the original port; this comparison changes that part of the path while retaining the printer, cable, outlet and application.

An authorized staff member runs one 40-minute after-hours session. Prerequisites are an accessible spare compatible port and recognition of the printer without installation or administrator access. If either is absent, this route is unavailable. Start only after staff confirm no pending client jobs or uncollected output. Use blank or explicitly synthetic pages and observe aggregate queue status without opening document entries.

First send two separate synthetic jobs through the original port. Account for both pages. With the queue empty, move the existing cable to the alternative port, keeping cable support and slack as similar as possible. If an installation or elevation prompt appears, stop and restore the original connection. Otherwise repeat the same jobs and idle interval, then return to the original port and repeat. Restore the starting arrangement after the comparison unless the alternative earns provisional use.

At a stall, record printer power indicators and queue progress before changing anything. Cancel only reconciled synthetic work if ordinary controls permit; retry after cancellation, then after reopening the application. These distinguish queue/application-sensitive recovery. Port-associated differences support a host-port or connection-path explanation. If both ports fail, a normal printer restart with the queue empty probes device/reset sensitivity; it cannot establish an outlet fault.

For opening day, use the alternative port only if ordinary printing works there repeatedly. Verify with a synthetic page, submit work individually, and pause for authorized reconciliation before any resend. Defer printing if readiness or output status remains uncertain.
candidates.experiment: Compare original�Calternative�Coriginal using identical synthetic jobs and similar idle periods. Original-port failure, alternative-port success and renewed original-port failure support provisional port avoidance; failures on both reject its sufficiency. No reproduced failure means no demonstrated benefit. Stop at 40 minutes or uncertain job status. Cable movement remains a confound, and cable defects, electrical quality and driver internals remain untested.

candidates.title: Remove a persistent queue processing block before resetting hardware
candidates.proposal:
Test whether an ordinary queue control is preventing dispatch. A selected ��Pause printing�� or ��Use printer offline�� setting, where exposed by the operating system, can inhibit printing despite a connected, powered printer. Clearing an observed processing block changes queue policy rather than canceling a job or resetting the USB connection.

An authorized staff member reserves 30 minutes after hours. This route requires a visible, explicitly selected pause/offline control that the current user can change. A generic ��Offline�� status alone is insufficient: it may simply report an underlying connection failure. If no such control exists, report this explanation as untestable through the available interface.

Begin with staff-confirmed absence of client jobs and uncollected pages. Record the original control states, printer power indicators and aggregate queue status. Send one blank or synthetic page. If it remains queued and an explicit processing block is selected, change only that control and observe whether the same pending synthetic job prints. If two blocks are selected, clear them separately, observing after each. Do not open client documents, clear the whole queue or change drivers.

If dispatch remains blocked, reconcile and cancel only the synthetic job using ordinary controls, retry, then reopen the test application and retry. With the queue empty, reseat the existing cable and repeat; finally try a normal printer restart at the existing outlet. Record these as separate queue, application, connection and device/reset observations. Stop when cancellation or output accounting is uncertain. Cable reseating and power cycling provide limited evidence, not proof of defective components.

After testing, restore original controls with an empty queue unless staff deliberately retain a demonstrated correction. Next day, check the identified control before accepting work and verify printing with a synthetic page. If it becomes selected again, restore processing only after pending jobs and output have been reconciled. Otherwise use the shortest supported recovery or defer printing.
candidates.experiment: The smallest comparison is one stalled synthetic job before and after clearing an actually observed control, without resubmitting it or touching hardware. Continued stalling falsifies that control as a sufficient explanation. Follow with two separate synthetic jobs. Do not deliberately create a pause and treat its predictable effect as evidence about earlier incidents. No observed block means no supported diagnosis; rare transport faults and the reason a control changed remain unresolved.

candidates.title: Use a printer-generated page to isolate the computer from the fault
candidates.proposal:
Test whether the printer can produce its own synthetic page while physically disconnected from USB. This removes the computer, application, queue and cable from the active printing path, providing a device-side comparison that computer-generated test pages cannot provide.

Prerequisite: the printer already exposes a clearly identified, ordinary-user command for a built-in synthetic test or demonstration page. Do not guess button combinations or use commands that print stored jobs or configuration details. If no suitable command is available, this alternative is unavailable. It otherwise needs only the stated equipment and one authorized staff member for a 40-minute after-hours session.

Begin after staff confirm an empty queue and no outstanding client output. Observe counts and status without opening document details. Record the original connections. Disconnect USB, print one local synthetic page, reconnect the same cable to the same port, and print one application-generated synthetic page. Keep the outlet and settings unchanged.

If computer printing fails, record queue progress and printer power indicators. Cancel only the synthetic job if permitted, reconcile output, and retry once; then reopen the test application and retry. These separately probe queue-sensitive and application-sensitive recovery. Stop if pending output cannot be reconciled.

With the queue empty, disconnect USB and repeat the local test before restarting the printer. Local success supports investigating the computer or connection path; local failure also implicates printer-side state or power. Reconnect firmly and retry computer printing to probe connection-sensitive recovery. Finally, with no pending work, perform a normal printer power cycle and repeat both tests. Restore the starting arrangement.

For opening day, verify the actual application with a synthetic page. Use only a repeatedly supported recovery. If local printing also fails, defer client printing and arrange later maintenance; repeated computer resets have little diagnostic value. Pause and reconcile any uncertain client job before resubmission.
candidates.experiment: Compare the identical USB-disconnected local test before and during a reproduced incident. A failed local test weakens a computer-only explanation; successful local printing alongside failed computer printing weakens a complete printer or power-loss explanation. Repeat the informative comparison once within the session. Different page content and USB disconnection limit causal attribution; neither result identifies a defective component. If failure never occurs, report ��not reproduced.�� Unchecked: cable substitution, outlet quality and driver internals. Risk: intermittent faults may recur despite successful readiness checks.
